problem.text:
Alice and Bob play a game on a sphere which is initially marked with a finite number of points. Alice and Bob then take turns making moves, with Alice going first:
- On Alice's move, she counts the number of marked points on the sphere, $n$. She then marks another $n+1$ points on the sphere.
- On Bob's move, he chooses one hemisphere and removes all marked points on that hemisphere, including any marked points on the boundary of the hemisphere.
Can Bob always guarantee that after a finite number of moves, the sphere contains no marked points?
(A hemisphere is the region on a sphere that lies completely on one side of any plane passing through the centre of the sphere.)

cues.why_it_matters: Alice turns $n$ points into $n + (n+1) = 2n+1$: with $n = 5$, that is 11. To end the round below 5, Bob must remove at least 7 of the 11, more than half; taking just the bigger half, 6, leaves 5 again.
cues.how_spotted: Run the rule on a small count, say $n = 5$, and work out how many points Bob must remove to come out ahead.

cues.why_it_matters: For $n = 1$ Alice makes $3$ points. If Bob can put $2$ of the $3$ on the boundary circle, those $2$ count for whichever closed side he takes, on top of its open-side share.
cues.how_spotted: When the statement settles a special case on purpose, like points on the boundary, ask how a player could create that case deliberately.

cues.why_it_matters: For $3$ points, Bob needs a boundary circle through $2$ of them. The words any plane give him that freedom, since any $2$ points lie with the centre in some plane.
cues.how_spotted: Read a spelled-out definition word by word and ask what freedom each word gives: 'any plane' lets Bob pick the plane.

cues.why_it_matters: Bob's plan must work however Alice places her $n+1$ points, so with $n = 5$ test every idea against her hardest placement of the $6$ new points for Bob.
cues.how_spotted: Underline 'always' and ask who chooses what: Alice chooses where the points go.

goal.asked: The question is whether Bob has a way of choosing hemispheres that is sure to clear every marked point, whatever Alice does.
goal.answer_form: The answer is yes or no, with a proof: either a rule for Bob's choices and a proof that the points run out, or a way for Alice to place points so that one is always left.
goal.final_line_would_say: After every round there are fewer marked points than before, so after finitely many rounds there are none.

candidates.name: Monovariant: the count falls every round
candidates.from_first_principles: To show the game ends, find a whole-number count that falls every round: the count left after Bob's move. Alice turns $n$ into $n + (n+1) = 2n+1$, so Bob must remove one more than the bigger half alone guarantees to leave fewer than $n$. Points on the boundary are removed whichever side Bob picks, and the freedom to use any plane lets him aim the boundary through marked points, so try the great circle through any two marked points and delete the fuller closed side.
candidates.why: It answers exactly the question asked: a whole-number count that falls every round must reach zero, and every step comes from a phrase of the statement.

candidates.name: Take the fuller open side
candidates.from_first_principles: The two open sides together hold the points off the boundary, so one side holds at least half; taking it is the natural first try.
candidates.why: From $n = 5$ Alice makes 11, and the bigger half alone gives 6, leaving 5 where the round started; without the boundary points the count does not fall.

candidates.name: Find an Alice placement that survives forever
candidates.from_first_principles: If the answer were no, Alice would need a spread of new points that no hemisphere can cover; spreading them evenly is the natural first try.
candidates.why: Bob chooses his plane after seeing the points, so he can aim the boundary at wherever Alice puts them; test any spread against that before trusting it.

method.chosen: Monovariant: show the count left after Bob's move falls every round, with the extra points coming from the boundary rule.
